senses: A small oven or furnace, used for the calcination of sand and potash, and converting them into frit.
A surgeon specializing in brain surgery.
examples: With considerable difficulty, Blake Taylor, the neurosurgeon who operated on her, stopped the bleeding.

senses: A traditional Jewish marriage contract that outlines the rights and responsibilities of the groom in relation to the bride.
The box in which shoes are sold.
examples: In one shoebox he had a whole collection of seeds he had saved from last year.

senses: A simple musical instrument (a membranophone) consisting of a pipe with a hole in it, producing a buzzing sound when the player hums into it.
Able to be split.

An ultimate atom, or simple, unextended point; something ultimate and indivisible.

ety: From Latin monas (“unit”) (from Ancient Greek μονάς (monás), from μόνος (mónos), from Proto-Indo-European *men-). By surface analysis, mono- + -ad.

senses: An advocate of determinism.
ety: Borrowed from French déterministe, equivalent to determine + -ist.

senses: Chilled to the point of freezing.
One who receives an honour or award.
examples: He won Service Animal of the Year and was the only honouree to sit for the duration of his induction.

senses: A list of items of special interest (such as highest priority, likelihood, risk, or otherwise).
A list of banned items.
examples: There were 22 schools on the hotlist to close, consolidate or be turned around.
The federal government is proposing to add a number of substances to a hotlist that will prevent them from being used in cosmetics.

senses: The state, quality, or manner of being ethical.
examples: Some reformers and sociologists, though the majority stuck by the older internationalist ethicalities, began to adopt imperialist and group Social Darwinist views.

As compared to the numerous studies focused on the incidence of student-faculty sexual involvement, few researchers have examined student perceptions of the ethicality of this form of sexual intimacy.

senses: A trump card game played by four players in two partnerships with a reduced deck of 24 cards.
ety: Possibly from German Juckerspiel, name of an eighteenth-century Alsatian card game, itself apparently a compound of Jucker + Spiel (“game”). Likely a doublet of joker.

senses: A net dragged across the bottom of a body of water.
A heightened effort by law enforcement personnel undertaken in order to capture suspects.
ety: From drag + net, probably based on the model of Middle English draynet, dreynett (“dragnet”), Old English dræġnet, dræġnett (“dragnet”), equivalent to dray + net. Cognate with Swedish dragnät, Norwegian dragnett, from Icelandic dragnet.

senses: A red spot of the kind that appears on the skin of someone suffering from measles.
A tapeworm larva.
ety: From Middle English mesel, from Old French mesel (“leprous”), from Latin misellus (“wretched", "unfortunate”), diminutive of miser (“wretched, sick”), of unknown ultimate origin.

senses: A manufactured (manmade) object.
examples: An amalgam of cultures, these manufacts sometimes lean towards the East and sometimes towards the West and function as status symbol or as a distinct 'code', worthy of a very broad spectrum of communication.

senses: Easy to break into small fragments; brittle or friable.
Characteristic of a story; storylike
Abounding in stories; legendary
examples: All that sort of thing is very storyful, of course, but it does not concern this account.
Toledo, the venerable, the storyful, is bowed with the weight of centuries.
The excitements of a pair of knickers, muddied on the storyful pavement, set his mind on murderous trackings.

senses: A type of round, brimless cap with a soft top and a headband to secure it to the head; usually culturally associated with France.
ety: Borrowed from French béret, from Occitan (Gascon) berret (“cap”), from Old Occitan berret, from Medieval Latin birretum, from Late Latin birrus (“large hooded cloak”), from Gaulish birrus (“short cloak”), from Proto-Celtic *birros (“short”) (compare Welsh byr, Middle Irish berr). Compare biretta.

senses: Covered by jungle
examples: Until 1975, Samorn says, Sen lived with her family in Bo Pailin, a heavily jungled subprovince in southwest Cambodia.

senses: Provided, cooked, or stuffed with truffles.
examples: The steak was served in a truffled sauce.

Lisa, who was already irritated, played impatiently with the handles of the knives, and told her that the galantine was truffled, and that she could only include it in an “assortment” at three francs the pound.

senses: One of the chief divisions of a long poem; a book.
The treble or leading melody.
The designated division of a song.
ety: From Italian canto (“song”). Doublet of chant.

senses: Representing by means of a figure; emblematic.
Figurative, not literal.
ety: From Old French figural, from late Latin figūrālis, from figūra (“figure”).

ety: From earlier Bad Lands, calque of Canadian French mauvaises terres à traverser (“bad lands to cross”), itself a calque of Lakota Makȟóšiča (from makȟá (“land”) + o- (attributive prefix) + šíča (“bad”)).

senses: Synonym of Psalms, particularly when printed as a separate work from the Bible.

A rosary with 150 beads, used for reciting the Psalms in Catholic editions of the Bible.
ety: From Middle English psauter & sauter, from Old French psautier & saltier, from Latin psaltērium (“a kind of lute or zither”), from Ancient Greek ψᾰλτήρῐον (psăltḗrĭon, “harp”). Doublet of psalterion, psalterium, and psaltery.

senses: Not having commutativity of all elements under its operation.

ety: From Middle English morelond, equivalent to moor + land. Compare Old Norse mýrlendi (“moorland”).

Troutbeck station, 10 miles from Keswick, in the heart of wild moorland, is the most isolated on the line.

senses: A lack of imagination, discernment or long-range perspective in thinking or planning.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μυωπία (muōpía, “shortsightedness”), from μύω (múō, “to shut, close”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”) + -ία (-ía).

senses: One million million (10¹²) watts, an amount of power large enough to power an entire region with many cities. (Consuming 1 terawatt during a duration of 1 hour consumes 1 terawatt-hour of energy.).
examples: As of 2025, it was estimated that all of the power stations on Earth were collectively generating about 15 terawatts at any given instant.

examples: In the case of the Rio Blanco experiment, it is the seepage of gas which is considered to be the "worst possible situation" that might occur.

ety: From Latin aedīlis (“commissioner or magistrate”), from aedēs + -īlis.
